v.why: Under standard parameterization with Adam, wider layers amplify the effective function-space step at high LR and push the net past the stability cliff, whereas the opposite is plausible because extra width could smooth optimization and tolerate the large steps.

Tiny batches give very noisy gradients that wide layers accumulate across many more units, interfering with training, though the opposite is plausible because wide nets average out noise and fit faster.
Capacity is already supplied by depth, so extra width mainly adds optimization difficulty and overfitting, though wider deep nets could also be easier to train and so help.

Strong L2 on top of reduced width stacks two capacity restrictions and causes underfitting, though the opposite is plausible because narrowing could partly offset the over-regularization by making the L2 penalty less dominant per unit.
At mid LR near the divergence edge, narrower nets reduce the effective step and restore stability, though the opposite is plausible because lost capacity could cost accuracy.
Very wide nets have excess capacity that needs L2 control to avoid overfitting, though the opposite is plausible because wide nets generalize well anyway and Adam-coupled L2 may add nothing.

Large batches remove the implicit regularization from gradient noise, so explicit L2 fills the gap, though the opposite is plausible because large batches with few updates are undertrained and more L2 slows fitting further.
A single-hidden-layer net has little excess capacity, so stronger L2 causes underfitting, though the opposite is plausible because shallow wide nets may still overfit tabular data.

With low LR the weights barely move in 243 epochs, so the added shrinkage competes with slow fitting and leaves the model undertrained, though the opposite is plausible because Adam normalizes the L2 gradient and small LR makes it negligible.

At a fixed epoch budget, larger batches mean fewer updates, which compounds with small step sizes into undertraining, though the opposite is plausible because less noisy gradients could make small-LR steps more efficient.
Larger batches reduce gradient noise that would otherwise destabilize high-LR training, though the opposite is plausible because fewer updates at high LR can lock in a poor solution.

When explicit regularization is negligible, the smoother gradients from larger batches avoid fitting noise and are cheap, though the opposite is plausible because the noise from smaller batches is the only regularizer present and should be kept.
Shallow nets tolerate gradient noise and benefit from the extra updates per epoch, though the opposite is plausible because noise could add nothing to a net that already trains quickly.

Strong L2 already regularizes, so the added noise from smaller batches is redundant and pushes toward underfitting, though the opposite is plausible because more updates per epoch could help overcome L2 shrinkage.

Deep nets have a sharper stability cliff, so a one-step LR increase crosses it more often, though the opposite is plausible because deep nets with Adam may need larger steps to move through flat regions.
Narrow nets have a gentler effective step and can use a bigger LR to get out of undertraining, though the opposite is plausible because narrow nets are more fragile to noisy large updates.
Large batches mean few updates and low noise, so a larger LR compensates as in linear scaling, though the opposite is plausible because the extra step size can overshoot with no noise to help escape.

Tiny batches inject large gradient noise, so a lower LR is needed to average it out, though the opposite is plausible because many updates per epoch already make small LR sufficient and lowering it further just slows learning.

Mid-width nets are already in a stable regime, so lowering LR only reduces progress within the fixed epoch budget, though the opposite is plausible because moderate-width nets may sit close to the cliff and benefit from stability.

Width already supplies capacity, so extra depth adds optimization difficulty and overfitting without benefit, though the opposite is plausible because depth gives hierarchical features that width alone cannot.

raw:
**Eight practitioner assumptions, each negated**

1. Wider is safer or better, so widening always helps. Negated: at high learning rates, widening raises the effective step size under standard parameterization and hurts. Under this negation, widening is worse at high LR, with tiny batches, and in deep nets.
2. Larger batches reduce noise and so are better. Negated: with a fixed 243 epochs, larger batches mean fewer updates and undertraining at low LR, while at high LR they stabilize.
3. More L2 always regularizes usefully. Negated: with Adam, L2 is coupled into the adaptive gradients. It is useless or harmful when small-batch noise or low LR already limits fitting, and useful only when noise is absent (large batches) or capacity is excess (wide nets).
4. Lowering the LR is the safe fix near divergence. Negated: it helps only when something else (tiny batches, narrow stable nets) is not already supplying stability. It costs accuracy under a fixed budget in stable regimes.
5. Depth and width are interchangeable capacity. Negated: they are substitutes, so adding depth on top of width hurts through harder optimization.
6. Small-batch noise is an implicit regularizer that substitutes for explicit L2. Negated: noise and L2 are redundant, so reducing noise is fine when L2 is strong.
7. Raising the LR speeds up convergence. Negated: it only helps when the update count is limited (large batches, narrow nets). It hurts deep and wide nets, which hit the cliff earlier.
8. Edit effects are additive and independent of the parent configuration. Negated: the sign of an edit flips depending on a different field's band, through bottleneck, substitution, or interference.
